word:greek-nt:G0064.explanation: Agreuo means to catch or capture.

word:greek-nt:G0213.explanation: Alazōn means a boaster or braggart—someone who gives himself airs in a loud, flaunting way.

word:greek-nt:G0266.explanation: Hamartia means sin. In Scripture, sin is something that can be forgiven.

word:greek-nt:G0327.explanation: Anazēteō means to seek out or search for, especially when the task is difficult.

word:greek-nt:G0378.explanation: Anaplēroō means to fill up or make up what is lacking. It can also describe fulfilling a law.

word:greek-nt:G0521.explanation: This Greek New Testament word describes someone as “stupid” or “uninstructed”—a person lacking sound understanding or proper instruction. The two meanings overlap in portraying someone who has not learned or does not judge wisely. It functions as a description of a person’s condition, not as a personal name or title. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Timothy 2:23; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific force there.

word:greek-nt:G0594.explanation: The word means “acceptance.” It expresses the idea that something is received favorably or regarded as worthy of approval. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Timothy, where its repeated rendering is “acceptance.” Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains the receiving or approving of something. This word is therefore focused on acceptance itself, not on a person, place, or physical object.

word:greek-nt:G0639.explanation: This word means “be perplexed” or “to be puzzled”—to face something difficult to understand or decide. It describes a person who is uncertain, confused, or at a loss about what something means or what should be done. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including descriptions of people who are perplexed in different situations. The central idea is not merely lack of information, but mental uncertainty when circumstances or questions seem difficult to resolve.

word:greek-nt:G0712.explanation: Ariston means breakfast or a mid-day meal.

word:greek-nt:G0833.explanation: Aulē means a courtyard. It can also refer to a palace.

word:greek-nt:G0910.explanation: Baptist means the baptizer, and it is the title used for John.

word:greek-nt:G1041.explanation: This word means an altar, a designated structure or place associated with worship. It is a noun naming the altar itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 17:23. Its basic meaning is clear, while the precise significance of the altar in that passage depends on the surrounding context of Acts.

word:greek-nt:G1175.explanation: Deisidaimonia means religion in general. In a negative sense, it can mean superstition.

word:greek-nt:G1342.explanation: Dikaios means just or righteous. It describes Joseph as a just man and can also be used as a title for the Righteous One.

word:greek-nt:G1416.explanation: Dysis means to sink or set, especially of the sun.

word:greek-nt:G1463.explanation: Enkomboomai means to clothe oneself. In this use, it describes clothing oneself with humility.

word:greek-nt:G1544.explanation: Ekballō means to throw or put out. It can describe removing something, such as a speck, or expelling demons.

word:greek-nt:G1625.explanation: Ektrepho means to nourish or nurture. It can also describe bringing up children.

word:greek-nt:G1720.explanation: This Greek New Testament verb means “to breathe into” or “to breathe on.” It describes directing breath toward or into something, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at John 20:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a deliberate breathing action. The paired meanings emphasize breath as the central action expressed by the word.

word:greek-nt:G1782.explanation: Enteuthen means from here, from this place, or hence.

word:greek-nt:G1838.explanation: Hexis means use, habit, or practice. Here, use exercises the senses so they can discern good and evil.

word:greek-nt:G1867.explanation: Epaineō means to praise or commend.

word:greek-nt:G1885.explanation: This word means “province,” referring to a larger territorial area governed as part of a wider empire or political realm. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in Acts, at Acts 23:34 and Acts 25:1. Its meaning identifies the administrative region connected with a place or authority, rather than a person, event, or spiritual quality. The precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:greek-nt:G1962.explanation: Epineuo means to assent to or consent.

word:greek-nt:G2079.explanation: This Greek New Testament word is an adverb meaning “extremely” or “finally.” It intensifies a description by expressing the highest degree, or it can point to something happening at the very end. In the Greek New Testament it occurs once, in Mark 5:23. Which sense is intended depends on the sentence and surrounding passage, but the word itself adds the idea of extremity or finality rather than naming a person, object, or action.

word:greek-nt:G2093.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “readily.” It is an adverb, so it describes how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, thing, or action itself. It marks an action as being done readily. The word appears three times in the Greek New Testament, in Acts, 2 Corinthians, and 1 Peter. Its exact force in any one verse is determined by the surrounding sentence.

word:greek-nt:G2215.explanation: Zizanion means darnel, a weed that resembles wheat but is worthless.

word:greek-nt:G2361.explanation: Thrombos means a large drop of blood. It describes great drops of sweat falling like blood.

word:greek-nt:G2484.explanation: Iturea is the name of a region or territory. As a proper place name, it identifies a geographic area rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, the word occurs once, in Luke 3:1. The word itself supplies the place name, while the surrounding verse and passage provide the historical setting and explain how it functions there. Its meaning is therefore straightforward: Iturea refers to a particular region known by that name.

word:greek-nt:G2523.explanation: Kathizō means to sit down or be seated. It can also mean to set someone in a seated position.

word:greek-nt:G2556.explanation: Kakos means bad or evil in the broad sense. It describes evil thoughts and evil actions. It can also refer to harm.

word:greek-nt:G2637.explanation: This word describes someone or something slanderous—speech or behavior that harms another person’s name through damaging accusations. It functions as a description of people characterized by this kind of speech. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Romans 1:30, so its broader scriptural use cannot be traced through multiple passages. Its central meaning remains clear: being slanderous, or marked by injurious speech against others.

policy.futureRepairGate: Reopen only after a verified source-alignment, lexical-identity, or evidence-view correction materially changes the closed evidence.
policy.priorReviewerNotes: The lexical gloss supports “sail to,” but Luke 8:26 is supplied only with “arrived,” which does not directly support the exact sailing sense. Thus the sole claim lacks valid Scripture support.

word:greek-nt:G2714.explanation: Katenopion means before someone's face or in that person's sight.

word:greek-nt:G2835.explanation: Kodrantes means a quadrans, the smallest Roman copper coin. In one saying, it is rendered “penny” for the last coin that must be paid.

word:greek-nt:G2888.explanation: This word refers to “powers of the world” or “world power.” It describes power understood in relation to the world’s ruling or influential forces. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Ephesians 6:12, so its precise force there must be understood from that passage’s surrounding wording. Its central meaning remains a power connected with the world rather than an ordinary personal ability or strength.

word:greek-nt:G2996.explanation: Lasea is a name referring to a specific location in the Greek New Testament. The word is not a general description of an action, quality, or object; it identifies something by name. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 27:8. Its precise setting and significance come from the surrounding passage, but the word itself simply names Lasea rather than expressing an idea or action.

word:greek-nt:G3003.explanation: Legiōn means a legion, a term for a very large number, as in more than twelve legions of angels.

word:greek-nt:G3076.explanation: Lypeō means to grieve or be sorrowful.

word:greek-nt:G3151.explanation: This word means a “babbler” or “idle talker”—a person characterized by empty, unproductive speech. It points to someone whose words amount to talk without useful substance, rather than identifying a particular subject being discussed. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Titus 1:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on speech that is vain or merely talkative.

word:greek-nt:G3322.explanation: This word means “be in the middle” or “to be halfway through.” It describes something positioned at the midpoint or a process that has reached its halfway stage. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in John 7:14, so its normal sense is narrowly attested rather than broadly illustrated across many passages. The surrounding verse context is needed to explain exactly what is midway in that occurrence.

word:greek-nt:G3380.explanation: Mēpō means “not yet,” indicating that something has not happened up to a given time.

word:greek-nt:G3524.explanation: Nephalios means sober and temperate. It describes someone who is not intoxicated.

word:greek-nt:G3591.explanation: Onkos means a weight, burden, or encumbrance.

word:greek-nt:G3630.explanation: Oinopotes means an excessive wine-drinker, or drunkard.

word:greek-nt:G3692.explanation: Ope means a hole or opening.

word:greek-nt:G3726.explanation: This word means to adjure or command, expressing a forceful charge that calls upon someone to comply. It describes more than a casual request: the speaker places the other person under a solemn demand. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, in Mark 5:7 and Acts 19:13. Its exact force in either passage is clarified by the surrounding words, but its central sense remains a serious command or adjuration directed toward another person.

word:greek-nt:G3753.explanation: Hote means when, marking the time at which an event or action takes place.

word:greek-nt:G3854.explanation: Paraginomai means to come or arrive, as when someone comes to or reaches a particular place from elsewhere.

word:greek-nt:G3928.explanation: Parerchomai means to pass by or pass away. It can also describe disregarding something, as when judgment is passed over.

word:greek-nt:G4024.explanation: Perizōnnymi means to gird oneself. It can also describe buckling a belt around the waist.

word:greek-nt:G4091.explanation: Pilate is a personal name; it identifies Pontius Pilate, the governor.

word:greek-nt:G4129.explanation: Plethynō means to increase or multiply. It describes growth in number, as when the disciples multiplied, and can also describe something increasing, such as the word of God.

word:greek-nt:G4226.explanation: Pou means where, referring to a place.

word:greek-nt:G4253.explanation: Pro means before, either in front or earlier in time.

word:greek-nt:G4330.explanation: This word means to allow someone to go farther or to permit movement onward. It describes granting permission rather than forcing or preventing an action. In its only occurrence in the Greek New Testament, it refers generally to allowing progress, while the precise force in Acts 27:7 depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s basic sense is therefore permission to continue farther, not merely movement itself. [p03:word:greek-nt:G4330:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G4330:occurrences]

word:greek-nt:G4392.explanation: Prophasis means a pretext or excuse.

word:greek-nt:G4451.explanation: Pyrosis means burning or a fiery trial.

word:greek-nt:G4503.explanation: Ruth is a personal name referring to Ruth. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs once, in Matthew 1:5. The word itself identifies a particular woman rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. Its meaning is therefore the person’s name, and understanding the significance of her mention requires the surrounding biblical passage. The name is rendered “Ruth” in the available English translations.

word:greek-nt:G4576.explanation: Sebo means to reverence, worship, or adore. It can also describe people as devout.

word:greek-nt:G4622.explanation: Zion is the name of a hill. It can refer to Jerusalem. It can also refer to the heavenly Jerusalem.

word:greek-nt:G4680.explanation: Sophos means wise. It can describe people regarded as wise and God as wise.

word:greek-nt:G4745.explanation: Stoa means a colonnade or portico, a covered porch.

word:greek-nt:G4860.explanation: Sympsēphizō means to calculate or count together. It can describe counting the combined price of many books.

word:greek-nt:G4965.explanation: Sychar is a city of Samaria.

word:greek-nt:G4987.explanation: Sōreuō means to heap up or load.

word:greek-nt:G5001.explanation: Tagma means an ordered series or order.

word:greek-nt:G5108.explanation: Toioutos means such, pointing to a person or thing of the kind just described.

word:greek-nt:G5157.explanation: Tropē means a turning or change.

word:greek-nt:G5333.explanation: Pharmakos means a magician or sorcerer, one who practices magical arts.

word:greek-nt:G5346.explanation: Phemi means to say or declare.

word:greek-nt:G5405.explanation: Phoinix is Phoenix, a bay or port on the south coast of Crete.

word:greek-nt:G5540.explanation: Chresis means use or the manner of use.

word:greek-nt:G6017.explanation: This word means to deride or make fun of someone. It describes speech or behavior that treats another person with ridicule rather than respect. As a verb, it portrays the act of mocking, whether through words, tone, or conduct. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 2:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: to ridicule someone openly or dismissively.

word:greek-nt:G6048.explanation: This word refers to condemnation or judgment—the decision that declares someone liable or subject to a ruling. It is a noun describing the verdict or adverse judgment itself, rather than the act of examining a matter. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 25:15, and is rendered “judgment.” Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and legal setting, but its central meaning remains a formal decision of condemnation or judgment.
